title: Hubble Captures NGC 2276
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2276, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, P. SellAcknowledgement: L. Shatz

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The trailing arms of the spiral galaxy NGC 2276 fill this Hubble image, a delicate pattern of bright spiral arms and dark dust lanes. It lies in the constellation of Cepheus.
At first glance it looks like countless other spirals. A closer look, though, shows that the galaxy is strangely lopsided, as if one side had been pushed or pulled out of balance.

Two forces have shaped it. One is gravitational interaction, the pull between galaxies, which can bend and stretch a spiral's arms. The other is intense star formation, which can light up one part of a galaxy more than another. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged it using filters from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared, which help reveal where young stars are forming.
scale: The galaxy lies about 120 million light-years away, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail without a telescope.
